title: The Language of Anderlecht
premise: Zephyrine Hartwell, a Brussels letter-writer who composes unsent postcards to her mother's burned-down address in Anderlecht, is hired by Odile, the last fluent speaker of a fading Brabantian dialect, to become her final student. As Zephyrine learns the language, she discovers Odile was her mother's closest friend — and the stranger in the old photographs her mother refused to explain, a woman whose silence after a betrayal broke them apart. When Odile's memory begins to fail, Zephyrine must choose between protecting her mother's version of the past and telling the truth that might reconcile them; in the end, she records Odile's stories, forgives the stranger in the photographs, and finally mails her postcards — to Odile, alive, across the table.
about_author: Xanthe Vane is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing letters no one ever claimed. She writes from a canal-side flat in Brussels, where she collects dying words the way others collect stamps.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. We meet her in her Brussels shop, Letter & Ash, where she writes letters for strangers and privately composes postcards to her mother's demolished house in Anderlecht. The beat is quiet loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: A Client Who Wants to Learn, Not Send
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. An imperious old woman, Odile Verstraeten, arrives asking not for a letter but for lessons in Marols, the Anderlecht dialect she is the last to speak. Zephyrine refuses; the beat is irritation masking recognition.

chapters.title: The Photograph on the Counter
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Odile leaves behind an old photograph of three young women outside the burned house. Zephyrine recognizes her mother and a stranger she's never been able to name. The beat is vertigo — her private grief suddenly has witnesses.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Burnt Address
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, flashback woven in. We see her ritual: writing to the dead address since the funeral, never mailing them. The beat is the weight of everything she never asked her mother.

chapters.title: Terms of the Lesson
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Odile's alternating POV. They negotiate lessons at Odile's Anderlecht flat: three afternoons a week, no questions about the past. The beat is a truce between two guarded people.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Her first Marols lesson — the word for hearth, for neighbor, for forgive. Odile teaches with a drill sergeant's cruelty and a grandmother's tenderness. The beat is reluctant delight.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. In a corner café, local shopkeeper Bram warns her that Odile's stories change depending on the day — and that her mother and Odile were inseparable once, then suddenly weren't. The beat is the first crack in the no-questions pact.

chapters.title: The Year of the Fire
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile remembers — imperfectly — the night the house burned, thirty years ago, and a quarrel in the street beforehand. She tells Zephyrine nothing. The beat is guilt rehearsed so long it has gone smooth.

chapters.title: Homework in a Dead Language
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine practices Marols by translating her unsent postcards, and finds the dialect has no future tense for 'I miss you' — only constructions of waiting. The beat is language reshaping grief.

chapters.title: Odile's Cabinet of Small Betrayals
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile catalogs her own unsaid things: a sister who emigrated, a lover who left, and a best friend she wronged. The reader begins to see the shape of the secret. The beat is complicity with the reader.

chapters.title: The Stranger Has My Mother's Laugh
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Studying the photograph, Zephyrine realizes the unknown third woman is laughing at something her mother said — intimacy frozen in silver nitrate. The beat is jealousy of the dead.

chapters.title: A Letter Arrives for Odile
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A solicitor's letter: a developer wants Odile's house, the last on the row, and Odile must decide within weeks. The beat is mortality arriving in bureaucratic form.

chapters.title: Marols for Goodbye
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile teaches the dialect's farewell formula, which literally means 'until the lamp is lit for you.' She privately admits she is losing words daily. The beat is fear disguised as pedagogy.

chapters.title: Zephyrine Asks One Question
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Breaking the pact, Zephyrine asks about the photograph. Odile goes silent, then furious, and dismisses her. The beat is the truce shattering.

chapters.title: What Bram Saw in 1994
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, one-off. Bram recalls the fire night: two women screaming at each other in Marols he half-understood, one word recurring — 'betrayed.' The beat is the past pressing through the present.

chapters.title: The Empty Flat
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. A week of no lessons. Zephyrine translates her mother's few surviving letters into Marols and finds a phrase her mother used — a dialect idiom she could only have learned from a native speaker. The beat is evidence accumulating against silence.

chapters.title: Odile Forgets a Word
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In the middle of a sentence, the Marols word for 'window' is simply gone. Odile writes it on cards and tapes them around her flat. The beat is terror managed by ritual.

chapters.title: Reconciliation Attempt, Failed
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine returns with pastries and an apology; Odile lets her in but deflects every question with grammar drills. The beat is forgiveness offered and refused, both directions.

chapters.title: The Developer's Offer, Again
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. The developer escalates; Bram urges Odile to sell; Odile digs in — the house is the only place the language still lives in the walls. The beat is loyalty to a place versus survival.

chapters.title: Odile's Version, Part One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile begins telling the story aloud to her tape recorder, alone: she and Zephyrine's mother, Margriet, were like sisters; the third woman in the photograph was Margriet's sister, Lien. The beat is confession begun.

chapters.title: Odile's Version, Part Two
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The betrayal: Odile, drowning in debt, secretly sold Margriet's family letters — including Lien's last letters before her emigration — to a collector. Margriet found out the night of the fire. The beat is the truth, ugly and human.

chapters.title: Zephyrine Reads the Collector's Catalogue
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Researching Marols for lessons, Zephyrine finds a private collection catalogue listing 'Correspondence of the Verstraeten-Hartwell families, 1960–1994.' The beat is the past surfacing on its own schedule.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Hearth
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Odile's alternating POV. Zephyrine confronts Odile; Odile, mid-fog of memory loss, sometimes confesses and sometimes denies, in the same afternoon. The beat is trying to argue with someone disappearing.

chapters.title: Margriet's Silence
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Re-reading her mother's letters, Zephyrine realizes Margriet never told her daughter any of it — protected her, or punished Odile, or both. The beat is anger at the mother, grief for the friend.

chapters.title: The Word Cards Fade
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile's taped word cards multiply; she begins addressing Zephyrine by Margriet's name. The beat is the clock now audible in every scene.

chapters.title: An Archive in Antwerp
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine travels to the collector's estate, now a foundation, and negotiates to see the letters. She reads Lien's last letter — and finds Margriet's furious marginalia, and, later, a draft of a reconciliation note never sent. The beat is the discovery that her mother wanted to forgive.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter, Mirrored
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine recognizes her own postcard ritual in her mother's unsent reconciliation draft — two generations writing to people who stopped answering. The beat is inheritance, named at last.

chapters.title: Odile Disappears
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Odile wanders off in a fog and is found at the burned house's empty lot, speaking Marols to the rubble. The beat is crisis — the language outliving the memory.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Bram's POV. The doctor gives Odile perhaps a year of coherent language, less of coherent memory. Zephyrine proposes recording everything. Odile refuses: memory is not a museum. The beat is the ethics of saving someone.

chapters.title: Loyalty vs. Truth
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine weighs it: tell Odile the full truth of what she did, or let her live in a kinder version? Bram argues for mercy; Zephyrine's mother's draft argues for truth. The beat is the book's moral hinge.

chapters.title: The Recording Sessions Begin
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. They compromise: Zephyrine records Odile speaking Marols — stories, recipes, insults, prayers — but never about the betrayal. The sessions become the found family neither expected. The beat is warmth earned through damage.

chapters.title: Odile Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile tells the fire story again, but now she's the hero and Margriet the betrayer. Zephyrine says nothing. The beat is the cost of mercy — carrying a false story so someone else can rest.

chapters.title: The House Is Sold
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Odile, in a lucid morning, signs the sale — on one condition: the buyer preserves the hearth wall, where she and Margriet once scratched their names as girls. The beat is letting go of place while keeping what it held.

chapters.title: What Was Scratched in the Brick
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. During the house's clearing, Zephyrine finds the names — and beneath them, a third name and a Marols phrase: the childhood oath the three women swore. The beat is evidence that the bond predates the betrayal.

chapters.title: The Oath, Translated
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine translates the oath: 'What is broken between us stays ours.' She realizes forgiveness was always the dialect's native tense. The beat is the thematic key turning.

chapters.title: Telling Odile the Truth
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Odile's POV. Zephyrine tells Odile everything — the letters, the sale, the fire. Odile, lucid for one long hour, listens, weeps, and says in Marols: 'Then she waited for me to say it first.' The beat is the climax: truth given and received.

chapters.title: The Letter Odile Writes
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Odile dictates a letter to the dead Margriet; Zephyrine writes it down, then — for the first time — mails it, to the foundation archive, to be kept with Margriet's papers. The beat is unsaid things finally said and sent.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Odile teaches Zephyrine the dialect's blessing for a new speaker. Odile's memory is mostly gone, but the language holds; she corrects Zephyrine's grammar with her old fierceness. The beat is transmission complete.

chapters.title: Postcards, Mailed
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Zephyrine mails her thirty years of postcards — not to the burnt address, but to Odile's new care home, one a week, in Marols, so the language keeps arriving. The beat is grief converted into practice.

chapters.title: Until the Lamp Is Lit for You
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, coda. A year later: the hearth wall preserved in the new building, the recordings archived, Odile gone but her voice on tape correcting Zephyrine's accent. Zephyrine lights a lamp in the shop window and teaches Marols to two neighborhood kids. The beat is belonging — found, kept, and handed on.
